grandparents.lede: Born in a farm house at Buckhorn, Oklahoma, Bob jumped out of airplanes for the U.S. Army for twenty years and came home to Choctaw County.
Margie Bell grew up on a farm outside Sherman, Texas, the daughter of Wayne and Melba Bell. She married Bob Johnson about 1962 and went with him around the world.
A Winona carpenter's son who married at twenty in front of 350 guests, raised five children along the Mississippi, and was killed on a La Crosse highway at thirty-eight.
The Rollingstone insurance agent's daughter who was widowed twice in two years, kept five children together, and worked at a La Crosse nursing home until the cancer that killed her at forty-seven.

stories.title: Twenty years and countless jumps
stories.hook: Bob Johnson left the Oklahoma farm country, became a paratrooper, served in Vietnam and twice in Korea, and retired a Warrant Officer 3.
body: Bobby Joe Johnson was born on 17 July 1937 at Buckhorn, a farm community in southeastern Oklahoma, the son of Joel Gilbert "Joe" Johnson and Nettie Beatrice (Tyson) Johnson. His obituary says he spent most of his youth "in the rural area of Southeast Oklahoma, a place that he loved dearly."

The 1950 census found him at twelve in a farm house on the road east of Sunkist, near Hunter in Choctaw County, with his father Joe, his father's wife Opal, a stepbrother Dan (Don Wayne Wilson), and two little half-sisters. His own mother, Nettie, had remarried Bob Tillery; her son Y. Q. Tillery was another half-brother.

Bob finished high school at Savoy, Texas, and went on to Decatur Baptist College, but "it became clear another path was destined for Bob, as he soon joined the Army to begin a new adventure." Not long after he enlisted he met Marjorie "Margie" Bell, and they were married for sixty-two years.

The Army sent him all over the United States and to Germany. He served one tour in Vietnam and two in Korea, became a paratrooper, and after "twenty years and countless jumps" retired as a Warrant Officer 3. He went home to the place he loved most.

In retirement he read military biographies, watched westerns and kept his yard and his vehicles immaculate. His family remembered his uniform for civilian life: button-up shirts rolled to the elbows, starched jeans, cowboy boots and one of his many Airborne hats. It was a daily thing for him to ask Margie if they could go and get the grandkids.

Bob and Margie had three children, Joey, David and Leatha. Their son David Glenn Johnson died in 1988 at twenty-four. Bob died on 28 September 2024 at eighty-seven, and was buried at Restland Cemetery, Boswell, where his father lies.

quotes.t: He became a paratrooper, and after twenty years and countless jumps, Bob retired from the US Army as a Warrant Officer 3 and returned to the place he loved most, Oklahoma.

src: Obituary of Bobby Joe Johnson, Miller & Miller Funeral Home, Boswell, Okla., Sept. 2024 (millerandmillerfuneralhome.com/obituaries/bobby-johnson)
1950 U.S. census, Hunter, Choctaw Co., Okla., dwelling 36 (Ancestry)

stories.title: Joe Johnson of the Boehler route
stories.hook: A Soper-born stockman who built airfields in World War II and married two Tyson women.
body: Joel Gilbert Johnson, always called Joe, was born at Soper in Choctaw County on 24 July 1908, the son of Joel A. Johnson and Winnie Bozarth. Soper was six years old, a cotton town that grew up beside the new Arkansas and Choctaw Railway.

When he registered for the draft on 16 October 1940 he was thirty-two, living at Boehler in Atoka County, working for himself, 5 feet 8 and 180 pounds, with a ruddy complexion, black hair and brown eyes. The person who would always know where to find him was his father, Joel.

He enlisted on 25 May 1942 and served until 21 October 1945 as a Technician Fifth Grade in the 872nd Engineer Aviation Battalion, one of the units that carved airfields out of jungle and farmland for the Army Air Forces.

His first wife was Nettie Beatrice Tyson, the mother of Bob, born in 1937. By the 1950 census Joe was farming near Hunter with Opal Tyson as his wife; the Arkansas marriage records also show Joel Gilbert Johnson, sixty, marrying Opal Wilson in Sevier County on 3 December 1968. His obituary calls her "the former Opal Tyson."

Joe died on Saturday morning, 25 November 1972, at his home on the Boehler route near Boswell, "after an apparent heart attack." The Paris News called him a World War II veteran, a member of the American Legion at Boswell and "a former stockman." His funeral was held at the Church of Christ in Boswell and he was buried at Restland Cemetery, where his government headstone records his war service.

quotes.t: Johnson, whose home was on the Boehler Route, Boswell, died Saturday morning after an apparent heart attack.

stories.title: Wayne and Melba Bell's farm
stories.hook: Married at Van Alstyne in 1937, the Bells farmed outside Sherman and Denison for forty years.
body: Wayne Douglas Bell was born at Anna, Collin County, Texas, on 18 April 1914, the son of Charles Hercules "Lee" Bell and Mary Alice Baker. Melba Nena Williams was born at Van Alstyne on 13 March 1918, the daughter of Cleave and Willie (Parker) Williams. They were married at Van Alstyne on 18 September 1937.

In 1940 they were renting a farm on Worchester Road in Grayson County with their first baby, a daughter. Wayne was twenty-six, 5 feet 10, 175 pounds, with brown hair and gray eyes, and when he registered for the draft that October he worked for Kimble Farms Inc.
By 1950 they were still farming in Grayson County, with daughters Sue, eleven, and Margie, seven, Rachel's grandmother. Two young Scharffer children, Glenn and Norma, were living with them too.

Wayne came from a big family. When one of his sisters died in 1968 the paper listed four sisters and four brothers still living: Ora Bell Russell, Mrs. J. R. Chapman, Mrs. Cecil Field and Mrs. S. W. Turner; and Charlie Bell of Van Alstyne, Wayne of Denison, Jack of Galesburg, Illinois, and Hardy of Anna.
Melba was a member of Cherry Mound Baptist Church. She died at home in Denison on 22 September 1981, aged sixty-three, and was buried at Van Alstyne. Wayne died on 22 July 1991.

quotes.t: She was a member of Cherry Mound Baptist Church. She married Wayne Bell, Sept. 18, 1937 in Van Alstyne.

stories.title: A reception for 350 on the Rivers lawn
stories.hook: David Nelton and Diane Rivers were married at Rollingstone on 26 July 1958, and the Winona paper printed every detail.
body: On Saturday 26 July 1958 at 9:30 in the morning, Diane Rivers, eighteen, married David Nelton, nineteen, at Holy Trinity Catholic Church in Rollingstone, Minnesota. The Rev. George Moudry performed the double-ring ceremony and celebrated the nuptial Mass. The altars were decorated with pink and white gladioli and lighted candles.

Diane carried a cascade bouquet of white roses and a double orchid. Her father gave her away. She wore a gown of Chantilly lace and tulle over bridal satin, with a lace bodice, long sleeves, a sabrina neckline and a full floor-length skirt, and a veil of silk illusion falling from a cap of lace. Her pearl necklace and bracelet were a gift from David.

Her sister Mary Lynn Rivers was maid of honor, and David's sister Sandra was a bridesmaid. The organist was Miss Angela Rivers. Douglas Trainor of Winona was best man; Diane's uncle Paul Rivers was an usher, and her cousins served the Mass.

There was a wedding dinner in the Flamingo Room of the Hotel Winona and then a reception for 350 people on the lawn of the Edward Rivers home in Rollingstone. Diane had graduated from Holy Trinity High School and attended Winona Secretarial School; David was a graduate of Winona Senior High, had attended Winona State College and was working for his father, a contractor. After a trip to the Wisconsin Dells, the paper said, the couple would be at home in Minnesota City.

quotes.t: A cascade bouquet of white roses and a double orchid were carried by Miss Diane Rivers, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Edward N. Rivers, Rollingstone, for her marriage to David Nelton.

src: "Diane Rivers Becomes Bride," Winona Daily News, 15 Aug. 1958, p. 8 (Newspapers.com)

stories.title: Highway 53, 2:44 a.m.
stories.hook: David Nelton, assistant superintendent of the La Crosse YMCA, died after a head-on collision in February 1977. He was thirty-eight.
body: David John Nelton was born in Winona on 19 July 1938, the son of Arthur and Helen (Canfield) Nelton. In 1940 the family lived on Lake Park Boulevard in Winona; by 1950 they were in Minnesota City, where his father worked as a carpenter in building construction.

After the wedding in 1958 David and Diane lived in Minnesota City and then Houston, Minnesota, before moving across the river to rural Holmen, Wisconsin, about 1971. They had five children. David became assistant superintendent of maintenance for the La Crosse YMCA.

At 2:44 on the morning of Saturday 12 February 1977 he was driving north on Highway 53 near the George Street intersection in La Crosse when his car and a southbound pickup truck collided head-on in the south lane. He died at 3:13 a.m. at Lutheran Hospital. The Winona paper noted that his death and five others that weekend brought Wisconsin's 1977 traffic toll to eighty.

His funeral was held at Fawcett Funeral Home in Winona and at St. Paul's Catholic Church in Minnesota City, with a Rosary the night before. The Rev. Joseph C. Frisch officiated, and because the ground was frozen, burial at Oakwood Cemetery, Minnesota City, waited until spring. His pallbearers were Richard Hohensee, Wayne Valentine, Charles Neuman, John Brown, Hollis Donehower and Robert Rolbiecki.

quotes.t: Nelton died Saturday, Feb. 12, in a La Crosse hospital of injuries received in a head-on collision of his car and a pickup truck on Highway 53 near the George Street intersection.

src: "David J. Nelton," La Crosse Tribune, 14 Feb. 1977, p. 12 (Newspapers.com)

stories.title: Diane, widowed twice
stories.hook: Diane Nelton lost two husbands in two years, filed a sex-discrimination complaint against an employer, and died of cancer at forty-seven.
body: Diane Mary Rivers was born on 10 August 1939 in St. Paul, the daughter of Edward and Viola Rivers, and grew up in Rollingstone, Minnesota, where her father sold insurance. Her mother, Viola Frisch, had married Edward at Rollingstone in 1933 and was a charter member of the St. Theresa Society at Holy Trinity Church.

Diane married David Nelton in 1958 and raised five children in Minnesota City, Houston and then Holmen, Wisconsin. In January 1975 she was let go by her La Crosse employer, E.T.C. Inc., and she went to the state: on 31 January she filed a complaint with the Wisconsin Department of Industry, Labor and Human Relations charging that she had been dismissed because she was a woman. The hearing examiner found no evidence that the firing was based on sex and dismissed the complaint in December 1976.
Two months later David was killed on Highway 53. Diane then married Stephen Fasher, who died in 1978.

On 13 August 1983 she married Charles Antony in La Crosse, and they lived at Bangor, Wisconsin. She worked at Hillview Nursing Home in La Crosse until December 1986. Diane M. Antony died of cancer at St. Francis Medical Center on Friday 27 March 1987. She was forty-seven. After a funeral at St. Peter's Catholic Church in Middle Ridge she was buried in St. Mary's Catholic Cemetery at Bangor.

quotes.t: She charged her former employer, E.T.C., Inc., 432 Division St., with discrimination based on sex in her Jan. 24, 1975 dismissal by the company.

stories.title: Arthur Nelton, carpenter and fireman
stories.hook: A Winona-born carpenter who sat on the Minnesota City council, fought fires as a volunteer, and buried his only son.
body: Arthur R. Nelton was born in Winona on 27 October 1909, the son of George and Anna (Brose) Nelton, whose parents had come from Germany. His mother died in 1928, when he was eighteen.

On 15 August 1934 he married Helen B. Canfield in Winona. In 1940 they rented a house on Lake Park Boulevard with their son David; Arthur, who had a year of college, was a carpenter earning $1,800 a year. By 1950 they had moved to Minnesota City with David and their daughter Sandra.

He was a self-employed carpenter in the Winona area until he retired in 1979, a member of Carpenters Union Local 307, a past member of the Minnesota City council and of the Minnesota City Volunteer Fire Department. His son David worked for him before his marriage.

Arthur outlived his son by seven years and his wife Helen, who died on 30 November 1982, by two. He died at Lutheran Hospital in La Crosse on 7 October 1984 at seventy-four. His grandsons Dirk and Kendrick Nelton carried his coffin.

quotes.t: He was a member of the Carpenters Union, Local 307, a past member of the Minnesota City Council and a past member of the Minnesota City Volunteer Fire Department.

src: "Arthur R. Nelton," Winona Daily News, 9 Oct. 1984 (Newspapers.com)

stories.title: The Rivers family of Rollingstone
stories.hook: Edward Rivers sold insurance in a small Catholic village above the Mississippi; his wife Viola lived there all her married life.
body: Viola M. Frisch was born on 9 June 1905 at Oak Ridge, Minnesota, a daughter of John Frisch. She married Edward Nicholas Rivers at Rollingstone on 14 June 1933 and lived there the rest of her life. Edward was an insurance agent in the village.

Rollingstone was a Catholic farming village in the hills west of Winona, and the Rivers family filled the pews at Holy Trinity. When their daughter Diane married in 1958, the wedding party, the organist, the ushers and the reception helpers were nearly all Rivers relatives, and 350 guests came to the reception on the lawn of the Rivers home.

Viola belonged to Holy Trinity Church, was a charter member of the St. Theresa Society, and was a member of the ladies aid. She died in August 1975, survived by Edward, her daughters Diane Nelton of Holmen and Mary Lynn Dahm of Newport, Rhode Island, a sister, Gertrude Koetter of Minneiska, and eight grandchildren. Msgr. Frank Klein said her funeral Mass at Holy Trinity, and she was buried in the church cemetery.

quotes.t: She married Edward Rivers June 14, 1933, at Rollingstone where she lived all her married life. Rivers is an insurance agent here.

src: Obituary of Mrs. Edward (Viola) Rivers, Winona Daily News, 14 Aug. 1975, p. 2 (Newspapers.com)

stories.title: Cleave and Willie Williams, and a horse thief
stories.hook: Melba Bell's parents farmed at Van Alstyne. Her father's youngest brother went to Huntsville prison at seventeen for horse theft.
body: Grover Cleveland "Cleave" Williams was born on 1 June 1887 at Shiloh, Tennessee, the farm country around the old battlefield, the son of Thomas Henry Williams and Rebecca Jane Britton, who moved the family to Texas. Thomas and Rebecca are buried at Van Alstyne; their stone gives 9 February 1847 to 25 December 1933 for him and 14 February 1850 to 20 September 1927 for her.

Willie Parker was born on 13 January 1891 in Texas, the daughter of James and Amanda (Pipkin) Parker. She and Cleave married in Van Alstyne, and their daughter Melba was born there in 1918. Rachel's tree had Cleave and Willie swapped as father and mother; Melba's death certificate and her obituary both name Cleave Williams as her father and Willie Parker as her mother.

Cleave died on 5 December 1949. Willie lived another twenty-five years, a member of the Van Alstyne First Methodist Church, and died in a Sherman hospital on the morning of 18 November 1974, aged eighty-three.

Cleave's youngest brother George, born in 1891 near Mantua, is the subject of a family story written for the Van Alstyne cemetery pages. At seventeen he and a friend, John Leo Skipworth, were arrested for stealing a horse and George went to the state prison at Huntsville. The family legend is that he went calling on a girl, found another man had got there first, took the rival's horse and rode it to death. In prison he developed "sugar diabetes"; he was released and died a few weeks later, on 31 May 1911, with his parents at his bedside. He was twenty.

quotes.t: She was married in Van Alstyne to Cleave Williams, who preceded her in death Dec. 5, 1949.

stories.title: The Canfields of Canfield Springs
stories.hook: A Pennsylvania family were the first settlers of a Minnesota valley in 1855, and a spring still carries their name.
body: In the summer of 1855 Patrick McDonough and John Canfield became the first settlers of Highland township in Wabasha County, Minnesota. The 1884 county history says they "built small homes for themselves, installed their families therein, and went to work." John and his wife Margaret (Greer) were Pennsylvanians who settled where Canfield Springs now is, the first settlers in the upper part of Cook's Valley.

John Canfield was a community man. On 8 November 1857 the neighbours met in G. A. Cook's house to organise a school district and named him director. The first road in the township, laid out in 1858, ran between Appel's Mill and Canfield Springs. The couple farmed there the rest of their lives and raised ten children.

Their son John A. Canfield, born on 29 June 1848, settled at Kellogg and married Anna Hall, the only daughter of George W. Hall, a Pennsylvania-born furniture dealer of Wabasha. Anna's son James Garfield Canfield was born in September 1881, and she died the following February.
James Garfield Canfield himself died in June 1912 at thirty, when his daughter Helen, Rachel's great-grandmother, was a baby. Helen grew up to marry Arthur Nelton in Winona in 1934.

quotes.t: Patrick McDonough and John Canfield were the first settlers of this town. They came in the summer of 1855 and built small homes for themselves, installed their families therein, and went to work.

src: History of Wabasha County (1884), Highland township and sketch of George W. Hall, archive.org/details/historyofwabasha00hhhi

stories.title: Boswell and Soper, two railroad towns
stories.hook: The Johnsons and Tysons lived in Choctaw County towns that did not exist before the railway came in 1902.
body: Rachel's Johnson and Tyson families lived for four generations in the southern part of Choctaw County, Oklahoma, in the old Choctaw Nation: George Washington Johnson and Marjorie (Fail) Johnson died at Soper in 1932 and 1926, Joe Johnson was born there in 1908, Opal Tyson was born at Sand Bluff in 1919, and Cornelius Tyson, Joe and Bob Johnson all died at or near Boswell.

Soper is eleven miles west of Hugo on U.S. Highway 70. The Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History says that in 1902 "dwellings and businesses began to spring up" when the Arkansas and Choctaw Railway built through the area. The post office opened in April 1903, and by 1920 the town had 538 people, two banks, four churches and three cotton gins.

Boswell is older than its railroad. About two miles north stood Mayhew, where Choctaws settled after removal; Presbyterians opened a mission school there in 1839, and it became the court ground of the Choctaw Nation's Pushmataha District. When the railway came through in 1902 the businesses moved south to the tracks, and the post office was renamed for Amity V. Boswell, who surveyed the right-of-way.
The Boswell News and the Soper Democrat carried the towns' news for decades. A tornado destroyed most of Soper's brick downtown in 1960.

quotes.t: In September 1902 the postal designation changed to Boswell, in honor of Amity V. Boswell, who surveyed the railroad right-of-way.
quotes.c: Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture, "Boswell"

stories.title: Is the Johnson line related to a Vice President?
stories.hook: Rachel's tree runs the Johnsons back to Great Crossing, Kentucky, and the family of Vice President Richard M. Johnson. No record yet proves the key link.
body: Col. Robert Johnson (1745–1815) and Jemima Suggett of Great Crossing, Scott County, Kentucky, had eleven children. One was Richard Mentor Johnson, Vice President of the United States from 1837 to 1841. Another was Joel Johnson (1790–1846), who married Verlinda Offutt in 1817, founded Lakeport Plantation on Lake Chicot in Arkansas about 1831, and is buried in Frankfort Cemetery beside his brother Richard.

Rachel's tree makes Joel the grandfather of George Washington Johnson, who was born in Mississippi in 1851 and died at Soper, Oklahoma, in 1932, through a son called Jonathan T. Johnson (1824–1859). The geography is possible, since Chicot County and the Mississippi Delta are neighbours.

But no source names a Jonathan among Joel's children; the Lakeport records list Lycurgus, Julia, Betsy and Cyrus. Joel had a brother called John Telemachus Johnson (1788–1856), and the name may have been garbled in a copied tree. Until a record ties George Washington Johnson to Kentucky, this is a family lead, not a fact. The Scottish noble ancestry further up the same branch (the Earls of Annandale) is a well-known copied-tree error.
